summary: This Best Current Practice describes the structure, content, construction and meaning of language tags, such as those indicating the language of a document. It also covers registering values and private-use extensions. With RFC 4647 it replaced RFC 3066. It was later replaced by RFC 5646.

eli5.summary: Language tags are short labels, like name stickers, that say which language something is written in. This explains how the stickers are built and how new ones get approved.

subtitle: How to build and register the short hyphenated tags, like en-US or zh-Hant, that label which language content uses.

tldr.problem: Software often needs to say which language a document, page or user preference uses, including details such as script, region or dialect, in a way every system reads the same.
tldr.mechanism: A language tag is a series of hyphen-separated subtags (language, script, region, variants, extensions, private use) whose types can be told apart by length, position and content, backed by an IANA Language Subtag Registry with a registration process.
tldr.outcome: It is a Best Current Practice (BCP 47) that, with RFC 4647, replaced RFC 3066, and it was later replaced by RFC 5646.

today: RFC 4646 was obsoleted by RFC 5646, which is now the place to look for language tags. It is BCP 47 and, together with RFC 4647, replaced RFC 3066.

sections.title: Why Label Languages
sections.content:
People often need to identify the language of information. A browser can use the user's language preferences to select web pages, and tools such as dictionaries can be chosen the same way. Processing such as spell-checking, computer-synthesized speech, Braille transcription or high-quality print rendering can also depend on knowing the language of the content.

RFC 4646 specifies the language tag as the identifier, a registration function for the values used to build tags, and mechanisms for private use values and future extension. In combination with RFC 4647, it replaces RFC 3066, which replaced RFC 1766. Tags cover spoken, written, signed or otherwise signaled languages, including constructed ones, but not programming languages.
sections.eli5: Computers need to know which language a page is in, for example to pick the right dictionary or read it out loud properly. A short label does the job.

sections.title: Tag Syntax and Subtags
sections.content:
A tag is a primary language subtag followed by optional subtags joined with hyphens. Each subtag is alphanumeric and at most eight characters, and whitespace is not allowed. Tags are case insensitive, so mn-Cyrl-MN means the same as MN-cYRL-mn: Mongolian in Cyrillic script as used in Mongolia. The registry's capitalization is only recommended.

The order is fixed: language, optional extended language subtags, script, region, variants, extensions, then private use. A script subtag has four letters (sr-Latn). A region subtag is two letters from ISO 3166 or three digits from UN M.49 (de-CH, es-419). Variants are registered with IANA, and one starting with a letter must be at least five characters, while one starting with a digit must be at least four (sl-nedis, de-CH-1996).

Because each subtag type has its own length and content rules, a parser can classify the pieces without an up-to-date copy of the registry. The one exception is a fixed list of grandfathered tags from RFC 3066, such as i-klingon.
sections.eli5: A tag is like an address written from big to small: first the language, then maybe the alphabet, then the country. Upper or lower case letters do not matter.

sections.title: Extensions and Private Use
sections.content:
An extension starts with a single-character subtag (a singleton) allocated to a registration authority, and every singleton may appear at most once per tag. An extension must follow at least a primary language subtag, so a-value is not well-formed while de-a-value is. The Extensions Registry can contain at most 35 records.

Private use subtags follow the reserved singleton x and always come last. Their meaning is defined only by private agreement, and they are NOT RECOMMENDED for general interchange. A tag can even consist entirely of private use subtags, such as x-fr-CH, where fr and CH do not mean French or Switzerland without such an agreement. Some registry values are reserved for private use too, such as primary languages qaa through qtz and the region ZZ, and these carry more public information than a fully opaque tag.
sections.eli5: Some tag pieces are left open for friends to make up their own meanings. They only work if everyone agreed on them first.

sections.title: The IANA Language Subtag Registry
sections.content:
IANA maintains the Language Subtag Registry as a machine-readable text file of records separated by lines containing %%, with each line limited to 72 characters. The first record holds a File-Date. Each record has a Type (language, extlang, script, region, variant, grandfathered or redundant), a Subtag or Tag, a Description and an Added date. Optional fields include Preferred-Value, Deprecated, Prefix, Comments and Suppress-Script.

A Language Subtag Reviewer, appointed by the IESG, keeps the registry in step with ISO 639, ISO 15924, ISO 3166 and UN M.49, and forwards each record to IANA. Anyone else can propose a new language or variant subtag by sending a registration form to the ietf-languages list for a two-week review. Records are never deleted from the registry, and once a tag is valid it stays valid.
sections.eli5: There is one official list of all the allowed pieces. A reviewer keeps it up to date, and nothing is ever taken off it, so old labels never stop working.

sections.title: Choosing and Processing Tags
sections.content:
The guidance is to use as precise a tag as possible, but no more specific than is justified. For example, de may suffice for a German email, while de-CH-1996 is probably too precise. The script subtag should be omitted when it adds nothing, as with Latn on en, and the Suppress-Script field says when. If a registry entry has a Preferred-Value, use that instead, for example he rather than iw. The und subtag SHOULD NOT be used to label content whose language is unknown.

Canonical form replaces mapped values and orders multiple extension sequences by singleton, and comparisons MUST be case-insensitive. Tags have no fixed maximum length, but protocols that limit buffer sizes MUST allow tags of up to 33 characters and SHOULD allow at least 42. If a tag has to be truncated, subtags are removed one at a time from the right, for example from zh-Latn-CN to zh-Latn to zh.

Implementations can claim to be well-formed processors, which check the ABNF and that extension singletons do not repeat, or validating processors, which also check subtags against a stated registry date.
sections.eli5: Use the shortest label that still tells things apart. Say de for German, not a long label with every detail, and if the label has to be shortened, cut from the end.

sections.title: Security and Compatibility Notes
sections.content:
The RFC notes that language tags used in content negotiation might reveal a sender's nationality, which could identify potential targets for surveillance. A tag also gives no assurance about the characters in the text, so it says nothing about possible homographs. Because tag length is unbounded, implementations need to guard against buffer overflow attacks, and they should not mechanically depend on extension specifications being always reachable online.

Compared with RFC 3066, all earlier tags remain valid and the new rules only add constraints. The goals listed are compatibility, stability (a valid tag stays valid forever) and validity, meaning a tag can be checked as well-formed without knowing its meaning.
sections.eli5: A language label can hint where someone is from, so be careful who sees it. Old labels keep working, and a label never becomes invalid later.
